proposed_edges.relationship: McNeill and Carolyn Merchant co-edited the three-volume Encyclopedia of World Environmental History (2003–2004 original edition), alongside Shepard Krech III.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh publisher reading: Berkshire product page, Description, final paragraph, and Additional information, Editor and Copyright rows, names all three editors and dates the copyright 2004. The contemporaneous Routledge launch flyer hosted by Berkshire, PDF p. 4, identifies the same three editors and advertises July 2003; PDF p. 5, About the Editors, confirms their identities. Thus the original-edition year signals differ, and the sentence preserves that 2003/2004 ambiguity rather than silently choosing a year or using a later reissue. JSTOR first-edition book record also gives 2004. The encyclopedia articles and introduction remain unread. This is a co-editing relationship only; no common theoretical position or influence is inferred. Shepard Krech III receives shared credit but has no endpoint.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Peak Document and the Future of Historical Research (2020), McNeill explicitly borrows vocabulary from James C. Scott’s Seeing Like a State (1998) to warn that scholars simplify other disciplines into usable but misleading forms.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh AHA text: final hazards discussion, paragraph beginning Inadequate appreciation of the complexities of other disciplines, and note 41. McNeill includes himself among scholars who oversimplify other disciplines, calling this an equivalent of seeing like a state. Note 41 states: “This vocabulary comes from James C. Scott,” and cites Seeing Like a State (1998). The following paragraph acknowledges limits imposed by training and finite lifetimes. This is explicit conceptual borrowing in a methodological analogy, not a claim of personal mentorship or that Scott originated McNeill’s environmental history. Scott’s book was not freshly read. The address was delivered 4 January 2020; the existing environmental-history contribution edge does not name this person-to-person resource.

review.reason: Paragraph 'Inadequate appreciation of the complexities of other disciplines', with 'Many scholars—myself included'; note 41: 'This vocabulary comes from James C. Scott, Seeing Like a State ... (1998)'. Delivered 4 January 2020. Explicit borrowing, as bounded.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the introduction to The Climate of History in a Planetary Age (2021), Chakrabarty uses McNeill’s account of twentieth-century demographic, economic, energy, and resource expansion while connecting capitalist globalization with planetary change.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh licensed Everand preview of the 2021 book: Introduction, Intimations of the Planetary, subsection Capital, Technology, and the Planetary, opening paragraphs, specifically the paragraph beginning As a result of the spread of industrialization and continuing through note marker 8. Chakrabarty explicitly attributes the account to “historian John McNeill” and calls the twentieth century “a time of extraordinary change”; he then moves from the expansion figures to climate justice and the limits of capitalism’s history as an explanation. These are Chakrabarty’s own words, not a publisher synopsis. The preview has no stable print pagination; the numbered note’s text and McNeill work cited there were unavailable, so no identification with a particular McNeill book is asserted. The rest of the book is unread. This records a specific named use, not the origin of Chakrabarty’s planetary framework. The 2009 Four Theses text was separately searched and did not verify this relationship.
